newsitem.title: USA: Horry Cty, S.C., to approach infrastructure bank.
newsitem.headline: Horry Cty, S.C., to approach infrastructure bank.

text.p: South Carolina's new transportation infrastructure bank will hear its first project report Tuesday, a road funding needs overview from Horry County.
But bond issuance by the bank is still at least several months away, Debra White, comptroller for the state Department of Transporation, said Monday.

"The bank is just getting started in determining what the criteria for (project) selection will be," White said. "I don't have any idea that they're going to issue bonds any time soon. There are a lot of questions that need to be answered."

Among them are whether bonds for large projects should be issued all at once or in smaller series. She said the infrastructure bank probably would rely on the pool of bond counsel already used by the state treasurer's office.

State officials said when the infrastructure bank was authorized during the spring legislative session that easing severe traffic congestion in Horry County was a top priority. The county, which includes the busy Myrtle Beach area, is a top contributer of tourism dollars to the state.

Horry County Administrator Linda Angus was unavailable Monday, and other county officials said they did not know if the county would submit a specific funding request. They have previously estimated the cost for needed road projects, including urban bypasses, at $545 million.
The bond bank was created to leverage state, federal and local transportation funds, enabling the state to speed up badly needed highway projects.
It got a healthy $65.5 million infusion last week thanks to lawmakers' decision to give the infrastructure bank all unallocated surplus revenues from fiscal 1997.

Revenue projections for the year were initially estimated at $4.43 billion and then raised to $4.52 billion toward year-end. Actual revenues for the year, which ended June 30, came in at $4.59 billion.
Assistant Controller General Barbara Hevener said no one revenue stream accounted for the gain.
"It's just the better economy," Hevener said. "It was pretty well across the board."
Lawmakers allocated about $232 million of the surplus, leaving $65.5 million, or more than twice as much as previously anticipated, for the infrastructure bank.

The comptroller also forwarded $3.4 million, or 3 percent of the previous year's total revenues, into the state's rainy day fund as required by law, Hevener said. That fund is fully funded at $130.4 million, she said.
